newsitem.title: USA: Domenici says make-or-break week for U.S. budget.
newsitem.headline: Domenici says make-or-break week for U.S. budget.

text.p: The Senate's top Republican budget negotiator said Sunday he is optimistic about the chanced for progress on a budget agreement during this "make-it-or-break-it" week.

Senate Budget Committee Chairman Pete Domenici, a New Mexico Republican, said on ABC's "This Week" he believed people of both political parties appear more ready to put aside some of the rancor and confrontation that led to last year's budget impasse.
"I think the president knows that if he's going to leave a legacy at all, of any real significance, he has to get this done," Domenici said.

"And I don't believe he cherishes four years of confrontation with Republicans, with threats of closing government and the like," he said. "And frankly, I think an overwhelming number of Republicans feel exactly the same way."
White House budget chief Franklin Raines said he was optimistic that the two sides could reach a deal this year, after last year's stalemate.
"I'm cautiously optimistic that we can get a deal, but it won't be easy," Raines said on the same program.

Domenici agreed with Raines' assessment but said that if progress is not made this week, he will be forced to start trying to put together an alternate budget with backing of moderate Senate Democrats.

"I really feel that this is a make-it-or-break-it week," Domenici said. "If we don't ... really get on with this by the end of this week, then I believe in the United States Senate, I'm going to have to proceed, hopefully with the blessings of our leader, Trent Lott, to get a bipartisan budget."
His counterpart, House Budget Committee Chairman John Kasich said he was neither pessimistic nor optimistic about prospects for an agreement.
But he told NBC's "Meet the Press" that there is better rapport between the White House and the congressional Republicans this year.

"I feel a lot better this year about things," he said. "I like the people that we're talking with at the White House. We've developed a relationship, all of us, talking to one another, trusting one another. We didn't have that the last time. And that's the first big step towards reaching an agreement."
But Kasich also said the two sides have major hurdles to overcome on taxes and related budget issues.
Both sides have been grappling with whether or how to modify the Consumer Price Index, which many economists believe overstates inflation.
But Raines said that any moves to change the CPI should not necessarily be tied to the budget. "I think we ought to try to get accuracy, and whatever context it occurs would be OK with me," he said.
House Republican Leader Dick Armey of Texas, on CBS's "Face the Nation," again called for a cut on capital gains taxes.
"We can get a capital gains tax reduction signed into law by this president in this year that would probably cut it in half," he said. "I think that is reachable, that's possible."
He also said he thinks it is possible to end, or substantially reduce, inheritance taxes.

House Speaker New Gingrich on Fox News Sunday threw a tax amnesty proposal into the mix of tax changes he recommends including cuts in capital gain taxes and inheritance taxes and a $500 a child tax credit.

Gingrich said House Ways and Means Chairman Bill Archer was looking into "a tax amnesty proposal whereby people would have a one-time opportunity to pay up their back taxes, clear the boards and then would face stiffer penalties if they didn't take advantage of that amnesty."
He said the proposal would bring in several billon dollars.
